fields.title: Tavro: The Largest Client vs. Everyone Else
fields.summary: 14% of revenue asks for one thing, 38% asks for another. Renewal in ten weeks.
fields.decisionPrompt: What will you do this quarter?
fields.brief/role: You are the product manager of a small team.
fields.brief/company: Tavro is a fictional company of 35 people that sells a field service scheduling system.
fields.brief/context: Severnye Obyekty is your largest client, accounting for 14% of revenue, with renewal coming up in ten weeks. Their COO told your account manager that renewal 'depends on' custom approval workflows: every request above a certain threshold must go through their specified hierarchy of approvers. No other client has requested this feature. The head of engineering estimates it will take six weeks for two developers—almost the entire capacity of the quarter.
fields.brief/objective: Secure the renewal and not waste the quarter.
fields.brief/constraints: Two developers for the quarter, about eleven weeks of capacity. The renewal decision is made in ten weeks. No time to hire.
fields.brief/task: Choose a solution and justify it.
fields.learnTakeaway/title: A major client asks for a solution—find out the actual requirement
fields.learnTakeaway/body: Behind a feature description, there is usually an external compliance requirement, and it is almost always narrower than the description: five levels of hierarchy turn out to be just a manager's signature and a log entry. Checking 'are we making this reusable' separates work that remains an asset from work that becomes debt for years. And quarter capacity is calculated before taking on two commitments, not after.
fields.evidenceCards/0/title: What is known about the client
fields.evidenceCards/1/content:
Offline mode (working without connection): requested by 31 clients, representing 38% of revenue. Sales lost 9 deals over two quarters where offline mode was cited as the reason—about 60 million ₽ in new annual revenue. Support receives about 60 tickets per month from technicians in areas with no connection.

Approval workflows: requested by 1 client. A review of requests over two years finds 4 mentions of 'approvals', all of which refer to a simple manager signature, not a hierarchy.

Among the 31 requesting offline mode are two clients of similar size to Severnye Obyekty.
fields.evidenceCards/2/content:
From a conversation with the head of engineering:

«Six weeks is for full custom workflows: arbitrary hierarchies, thresholds by job types, out-of-office delegation, and logging. This is the version Severnye Obyekty described.

There is a much smaller one: a single customizable threshold and a fixed two-step workflow built on the existing approval mechanism. This takes about ten days, and it will be useful for everyone, not just them.

Offline mode is seven weeks, and it cannot be cut: half of offline mode is worse than none at all».
fields.evidenceCards/3/title: How it went in the past
fields.evidenceCards/3/content:
Tavro has twice built features for large accounts.

Two years ago: a custom report export for a client who left anyway after 14 months. The export is still maintained, nobody uses it, costing about one engineering-week per year in maintenance.

Last year: a custom permission model for a client who stayed. It was later generalized, and now three clients use it.

The difference between the two cases, according to the head of engineering: «In the second one, we built something generalizable from the start; in the first, we built it for just one client».
fields.decisionOptions/0/label: General version in ten days, then offline mode
fields.decisionOptions/0/description: Build a reusable approval system with one threshold and two steps, present it to Severnye Obyekty as the first release along with a roadmap, and secure seven weeks for offline mode.
fields.decisionOptions/0/consequence:
The conversation with the COO shows that the audit requirement is simpler than their description: an expensive request doesn't go to work without a manager's signature, and this is visible in the log. Five levels of hierarchy is their description, but only two actually work.
Ten days covers this completely, and the feature goes to everyone: four requests over two years were exactly about this kind of signature.
This leaves seven weeks for offline mode—what 31 clients and 38% of revenue are asking for, and why nine deals were lost.
Severnye Obyekty renews: they have a working approval system and a roadmap for the rest with dates.
The company's past experience is confirmed: last year's generalized version is used by three clients, while the custom export from two years ago is used by none, yet still maintained.
Compromise: the client does not get the full hierarchy with delegation, and you had to promise it in writing for the next quarter.
fields.decisionOptions/1/description: Tell Severnye Obyekty that the feature won't be delivered this quarter, protect the demand of 38% of revenue, and let the account manager handle the renewal.
fields.decisionOptions/1/consequence:
The priority based on numbers is chosen correctly: 31 clients vs. one, 38% of revenue vs. 14%, nine lost deals.
But the refusal was made before finding out what was behind the requirement—which was an audit that could be resolved with ten days of work.
The account manager handles the renewal without a single substantive argument; the COO, facing an outstanding audit finding, looks for a solution elsewhere.
The renewal goes through, but for nine months instead of three years, and with a clause about approvals in the contract.
Compromise: the correct priority was protected at the cost of a relationship that could have been saved with ten days of work.
fields.decisionOptions/2/description: Allocate six weeks to build their described version and postpone offline mode to the next quarter.
fields.decisionOptions/2/consequence:
Six weeks are spent on arbitrary hierarchies, thresholds by type, delegation, and logging.
The client is happy, and the renewal goes through. A month later, it turns out that only two out of five levels are actually configured—exactly what their own COO said.
Offline mode is pushed back by a quarter, and during this time, two more deals are lost for the same reason.
A year later, the story of the custom export from two years ago repeats: only one client uses the feature, and maintenance costs time every year.
Compromise: the commitment was fulfilled in the form they described, not the form they actually needed.
fields.decisionOptions/3/label: Split the team and do both
fields.decisionOptions/3/description: Assign one developer to approvals and the other to offline mode to avoid giving up on anything.
fields.decisionOptions/3/consequence:
Six weeks for two developers turns into twelve weeks for one; seven weeks of offline mode turns into fourteen.
By the tenth week, when the renewal is decided, the client has no working approval system; by the end of the quarter, there is no offline mode either.
The head of engineering warned directly: half of offline mode is worse than none at all.
Both promises are broken, and there is no way to explain it: capacity was known from the start.
Compromise: trying to avoid giving up on anything ended up giving up on everything.
fields.rubric/remediation/0/gap: An external factor is named but not carried through to its logical conclusion for the decision
fields.rubric/remediation/1/gap: A strength is claimed without proof and without what it limits
fields.rubric/remediation/2/gap: A competitor is analyzed by feature set rather than growth mechanism
fields.rubric/remediation/3/gap: Clients are not segmented by profit and cost of service
fields.rubric/remediation/4/gap: The financial decision was made without the math of pricing, churn, and expansion
